teaser: Nine people are having a wonderful evening. The tenth has just looked inside his shoe.
review_notes:
Date usually given as about 1665-1668; oil on canvas, 82 x 70.5 cm.
Doll held by the little girl: identified by the Rijksmuseum as John the Baptist.
Rod in the shoe: the twigs are faint in the working image, next to the shoe the sister holds at about x 0.35, y 0.48. Check on the zoom image.
Grandmother beckoning toward the bed curtain, implying a hidden present for the crying boy: standard reading.
Baby holding a gingerbread figure of the saint; younger boy holding a kolf club: standard readings, small in the image.
Apple with a coin pushed into it on the floor (about x 0.68, y 0.93): standard reading; the coin is not legible in the working image.
Diamond-shaped loaf leaning on the table: a 'duivekater', a festive white bread.
Signature 'JSteen' at lower right, below the loaf.
Steen was Catholic; son of a Leiden brewer; leased a brewery in Delft (1654); licensed to keep a tavern in Leiden in 1672. That he used his own children as models here is a tradition, stated as 'probably'.
Reformed opposition to the feast and local bans on Saint Nicholas markets and saint-shaped cookies (for instance Delft 1607, Amsterdam 1663): wording kept general, please verify.
Sinterklaas as the origin of the name Santa Claus: common account.

lesson.text: Count the smiles in this room. A little girl hugging a new doll, a mother with open arms, a grandmother, a father, a boy grinning so hard his eyes close. Then, at the far left, one face is crumpled, with a fist rubbing an eye. The happiest night of the Dutch year has made someone cry.

The date is December 5, the eve of Saint Nicholas. The custom was simple. Children set a shoe by the fireplace before bed. In the night the saint came down the chimney and filled it: sweets and toys for those who had behaved, and for those who had not, a bundle of birch twigs, the rod used for spanking.
Jan Steen does not show the saint, the night or the chimney. He shows the minute of discovery, and he lets you work out the verdict yourself, the way you would if you walked into the room.
The crying boy got something in his shoe. Someone else is holding it up for all to see. Find the shoe.

spots.title: The rod
spots.text: His big sister dangles the shoe at arm's length, a spray of thin twigs sticking out of it. She is smiling. This is the worst part of the punishment: everybody knows.

lesson.text: Steen was a storyteller before anything else, and he tells this one the way a good gossip would, by showing who is looking at whom. Nearly every gesture in the room points somewhere. Follow them and the plot appears.
Four gestures, four pieces of the story.

lines.label: The little brother
lines.text: The curly-haired boy stretches his arm across half the picture to point at the loser. In his other hand he clutches his own present, a club for kolf, an old Dutch game played with a stick and ball.

lines.label: The mother
lines.text: Her hands reach for the little girl: show me what you got. The girl twists away and holds her treasures tighter.

lines.label: The chimney
lines.text: At the back, an older boy carrying the baby points up into the fireplace. That is where the gifts came from, he explains. The child beside him sings up the chimney in thanks.

lines.label: The grandmother
lines.text: Half hidden by the bed, she looks toward the crying boy and crooks a finger. Her other hand is at the curtain. Something for him is waiting behind it.

lesson.text: That last gesture changes the mood of the whole scene. The boy has been taught his lesson, in public, and in a minute he will be forgiven. Steen was a moralist who rarely stayed stern for long. He preferred a family that teases to a family that punishes.

In Dutch, a noisy, messy home is still called “a Jan Steen household.” The expression comes from his many paintings of families in cheerful disorder, with pets on the table and children up to no good. This room, by his standards, is tidy.

He knew such rooms well. Steen was born in Leiden in 1626, the son of a brewer. He ran a brewery himself for a while, without much success, and late in life he kept a tavern. He painted this canvas in the 1660s, when he had a houseful of children, who probably posed for it.
The star of the evening stands in the middle, in the best light and the brightest dress. She has been very good, and her arms are too full to carry it all.

lesson.title: The good child's haul
lesson.text: Start with what she holds, then see what the saint left around the room.

spots.title: The doll
spots.text: Not a baby doll: a little bearded saint with a halo of spikes, John the Baptist. A holy figure as a toy tells you something about this family. Hold on to that.

spots.title: The bucket
spots.text: Over her arm hangs a pail crammed with sweets and small toys. Her satin sleeve glows orange. Steen, who could paint roughly when he wanted, spends his finest brushwork on her.

spots.title: The baby's cookie
spots.text: The smallest child grips a flat brown figure almost as long as its arm: a gingerbread Saint Nicholas, baked in a carved wooden mold.

spots.title: The big loaf
spots.text: Propped against the table, a diamond-shaped white bread pressed with patterns. This festive loaf was baked only for the weeks around midwinter.

lesson.text: All that bread and gingerbread is still on Dutch tables every December. The picture works almost like a recipe book for the feast: waffles and honey cake in the basket at the lower left, nuts and their shells across the floor tiles, oranges and candy on the table.

The saint in this party was not officially welcome. The Dutch Republic was governed by Protestants, whose ministers preached against honoring saints, and some towns passed rules against Saint Nicholas markets and cookies in the shape of the bishop. Families went on celebrating anyway.

Steen was a Catholic, a tolerated minority that had to worship in private houses. That may explain the doll. A girl hugging John the Baptist, a baby holding a gingerbread bishop: in this home the old faith is not hidden at all. It has simply moved from the church into the toy basket.
Steen paints a custom the way an insider sees it. Every object has a job in the story, and the story is told by glances and pointing fingers, with no single hero.

Technically, the picture is a balancing act. Ten figures share a canvas only 82 cm high (about 32 inches). Steen keeps them readable by running a loose diagonal from the weeping boy up to the hand at the chimney, and by leaving the foreground floor nearly empty, like the front of a stage. Nearly.

The feast crossed the Atlantic with Dutch settlers. In America the Dutch name Sinterklaas was gradually worn down to “Santa Claus,” and the gifts moved from December 5 to Christmas. The chimney, the night visit and the judgment of good and bad children all stayed.
The room is full of things you have not been shown yet. The floor alone holds a small mystery or two, and the painter left his name down there as well.

spots.title: The tears
spots.text: A big boy, nearly a teenager, with his hat still on, wiping one eye with his knuckles. He is too old to cry like this, which is why the others find it so funny.

spots.title: A lost shoe
spots.text: One shoe lies kicked over on the tiles, laces loose. It may be the mate of the one the sister is holding up.

spots.title: The apple
spots.text: An apple has rolled onto the floor. A traditional gift was an apple with a coin pushed into it, and this one is usually read that way.

spots.title: The basket
spots.text: Round buns, a crisp waffle, a long slab of honey cake studded with white almonds or sugar, and an apple. Steen paints each crust differently.

spots.title: The singer
spots.text: Head back, mouth wide: a child singing a Saint Nicholas song toward the chimney. Songs asking the saint to throw something down are still sung in the Netherlands.

spots.title: The father
spots.text: Seated in the middle in an old-fashioned ruff, he smiles into the distance and does nothing at all. In Steen's homes the adults are seldom in charge.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: In the shadow under the big loaf, in small brown script: JSteen, with the J and S joined.

lesson.text: Go back to the contradiction you started with. The crying boy is why the painting has lasted. A room where everyone is happy would be a greeting card. One child in disgrace, with rescue already on its way from behind the curtain, is a family.

quiz.question: What did a naughty child find in his shoe on Saint Nicholas's eve?
options: A bundle of birch twigs, the rod
quiz.explanation: The sister holds up the shoe with the rod sticking out of it.

quiz.question: What does the grandmother's gesture suggest?
options: A present for the crying boy is hidden behind the curtain
She wants the children to go to bed
quiz.explanation: She beckons to him with one hand on the bed curtain, so forgiveness is on its way.

quiz.question: Which figure does the little girl's doll represent?
quiz.explanation: It is a small bearded saint with a spiky halo, a sign of the family's Catholic faith.

quiz.question: Why was this feast awkward in the Dutch Republic?
quiz.explanation: The Republic was governed by Protestants, yet families kept the Catholic saint's feast.

quiz.question: What does “a Jan Steen household” mean in Dutch?
quiz.explanation: The phrase comes from his many pictures of families in cheerful disorder.

quiz.question: How does Steen mainly tell the story in this picture?
options: With a written caption on the wall
By placing the saint in the middle
Through glances and pointing gestures between the figures
quiz.explanation: Almost every gesture points to another person or to the chimney.

facts.text: Saint Nicholas himself appears in the painting, coming down the chimney.
facts.explanation: Steen shows only the family discovering the gifts; a boy merely points up the chimney.

facts.text: The name Santa Claus comes from the Dutch Sinterklaas.
facts.explanation: Dutch settlers took the feast to America, where the name was worn down.

facts.text: Jan Steen was the son of a brewer and later kept a tavern.
facts.explanation: He was born into a Leiden brewing family and ran a tavern late in life.
